sections.heading: An Aurora cluster runs DB instances on one shared cluster volume

plan.problem: A classic database ties its data to the disk of one server. A second server, or a bigger one, first needs its own copy of all the data. Aurora keeps the data apart from the servers.
trace: **One engine you know.** Aurora is a [fully managed relational database engine] (aurora-is-managed-relational-engine) that is [compatible with MySQL and PostgreSQL] (aurora-is-managed-relational-engine), and it is [part of the managed database service] (aurora-part-of-rds) Amazon RDS.

**Compute apart from storage.** A cluster has [one or more DB instances] (aurora-cluster-has-instances-and-volume) and [a cluster volume that manages the data] (aurora-cluster-has-instances-and-volume).

**One writer.** Each cluster has [one primary DB instance] (aurora-one-primary-per-cluster); the [primary instance handles all data definition language] (aurora-primary-handles-ddl-dml) and data manipulation statements.
**More instances are readers.** The other DB instances are read-only and are [known as Aurora Replicas] (aurora-replicas-read-only-auto-replication).

**Add an instance without copying.** You can [add a DB instance quickly] (aurora-add-instance-no-data-copy), because Aurora [doesn't make a new copy] (aurora-add-instance-no-data-copy) of the table data.
plan.table: What lives where (columns: Part | Holds | You change it by): DB instance | CPU and memory; the class [determines the computation and memory capacity] (aurora-instance-class-determines-compute-memory) | choosing another instance class; Cluster volume | [user data, schema objects, and internal metadata] (aurora-cluster-volume-contents-all-data-and-metadata) | nothing: it follows the data (subsection 3); Cluster | both, managed as one: Aurora works on [entire clusters of database servers] (aurora-management-operates-on-clusters) | adding or removing DB instances. One link per fact per cell; cells at most 15 words.
plan.why: Why keep compute and storage apart? An instance can join or leave without moving data, and you can delete DB instances while [preserving the cluster itself] (aurora-delete-instances-keep-cluster-and-data). Even a cluster with [only a single DB instance] (aurora-single-instance-still-a-cluster) is [still a cluster] (aurora-single-instance-still-a-cluster), because its storage already spans Availability Zones.
plan.exam_signal: "a relational database compatible with MySQL or PostgreSQL, with high performance and availability" points to Aurora, a [fully managed relational database service] (aurora-faq-what-is-aurora); "migrate or modernize an on-premises relational workload" also points to Aurora ([migrating or modernizing an on-premises relational workload] (aurora-dg-use-when-relational-modernize)).
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence: existing [code, tools, and applications] (aurora-existing-mysql-postgres-code-works) work with Aurora, with [standard MySQL and PostgreSQL database drivers] (aurora-faq-no-special-drivers). Reference only, no sentence: the throughput claim of up to 6x (aurora-throughput-up-to-6x-stock-mysql-and-postgresql: volatile marketing figure; the decision guide still says five times); T classes for dev and test only (aurora-t-classes-dev-test-only); query tuning stays with you (aurora-customer-responsible-query-tuning; chapter 26 teaches the split); Aurora PostgreSQL Limitless Database for write throughput [beyond the limits of a single Aurora instance] (aurora-dg-limitless-beyond-single-instance): name it at most once, never as a question key; Amazon Aurora DSQL is a separate service outside the exam's in-scope list (aurora-dg-dsql-active-active-multi-region): no sentence.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: Aurora puts several DB instances on one shared volume. The thing to watch is that one instance writes.
plan.stop_and_answer: A team adds a third DB instance to an Aurora cluster that holds 2 TB of data. Does Aurora copy the 2 TB to the new instance before it can serve queries? Answer: no; Aurora [doesn't make a new copy] (aurora-add-instance-no-data-copy) of the table data, and the new instance connects to the shared volume, so you can [add a DB instance quickly] (aurora-add-instance-no-data-copy). 2 TB is an example value.

sections.heading: Every write is stored as six copies across three Availability Zones

plan.problem: A disk can fail, and so can a whole Availability Zone. The data must survive both, and writes must keep working.
trace: **The writer sends each change to storage.** Aurora [synchronously replicates the data across Availability Zones] (aurora-synchronous-replication-to-six-storage-nodes) to [six storage nodes] (aurora-synchronous-replication-to-six-storage-nodes).

**Three zones, two copies in each.** The volume holds [six copies] (aurora-storage-six-copies-three-azs) of your data across [three AZs] (aurora-storage-six-copies-three-azs), all in a [single AWS Region] (aurora-cluster-volume-three-azs-one-region).

**Small pieces, fast repair.** Aurora splits the volume into [10 GiB segments] (aurora-storage-segment-size-10-gib); when a segment fails, [Aurora immediately repairs the segment] (aurora-storage-auto-repair-segment) from the other copies.

**Lost copies are absorbed.** Writes continue after the loss of [up to two copies] (aurora-storage-loss-tolerance-write-read); reads continue after the loss of [up to three copies] (aurora-storage-loss-tolerance-write-read).
plan.table: What keeps working (columns: Event | What happens): one disk segment fails | Aurora repairs it from the other copies (aurora-storage-auto-repair-segment, already linked in the trace: no second link needed); two copies are lost | reads and writes continue; three copies are lost | reads continue ([up to three copies] (aurora-storage-loss-tolerance-write-read)); the writer DB instance fails | storage is fine; the compute side recovers by failover (subsection 6). Write no row that states what happens after three lost copies for writes: no fact says it.
plan.why: Why six copies of one write? With copies in three zones, the chance of data loss from a disk failure is [greatly minimized] (aurora-three-azs-copies-minimize-disk-loss), and [you only pay for one copy] (aurora-faq-pay-for-one-copy).
plan.exam_signal: "the data must survive the loss of an Availability Zone without managing replication" points to the Aurora cluster volume: a cluster can tolerate the failure of an Availability Zone [without any loss of data] (aurora-cmp-ha-az-failure-no-data-loss-brief-interruption).
plan.exam_trap_text: > **Exam trap:** Six copies protect the data, not the DB instance. A cluster with no Aurora Replica recreates its writer, which typically takes [less than 10 minutes] (aurora-failover-time-without-replica). <!-- trap: aurora-trap-single-instance-is-ha -->
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: fast restarts (at most 70 words). After a crash, Aurora does not replay the redo log, which cuts restart time to [less than 60 seconds] (aurora-faq-crash-restart-under-60s) in most cases. It [recovers asynchronously on parallel threads] (aurora-recovery-asynchronous-parallel-threads), and the page cache is [managed in a separate process from the database] (aurora-page-cache-survives-database-restart). Self-repair also [reduces the need to perform a point-in-time restore] (aurora-auto-repair-avoids-pitr) after a disk failure.
plan.body_extras: Reference only, no sentence unless words remain: Aurora picks the three zones from the DB subnet group ([three separate AZs selected automatically by Aurora] (aurora-storage-three-azs-from-subnet-group)); every DB instance must be in one of them (aurora-every-instance-in-one-of-three-azs); the copies exist [regardless of whether the instances] (aurora-storage-copies-regardless-of-instance-azs) span zones; a subnet group needs [at least two Availability Zones] (aurora-db-subnet-group-two-azs); replication is free ([for DB cluster replication is free] (aurora-data-transfer-between-azs-for-replication-free)); Aurora [doesn't support Local Zones] (aurora-no-local-zones); SLA credit thresholds 99.99% Multi-AZ and 99.9% Single-AZ (aurora-sla-multi-az-99-99, aurora-sla-single-az-99-9) are service-credit terms, not an availability promise: no sentence.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: Aurora saves each write six times in three zones. The thing to watch is compute: one instance is still one instance.
plan.stop_and_answer: A cluster's storage uses AZ 1, AZ 2 and AZ 3, and its only DB instance runs in AZ 1. During the morning peak, two storage nodes in AZ 2 fail. Do writes stop? Answer: no; writes continue after the loss of [up to two copies] (aurora-storage-loss-tolerance-write-read), and [Aurora immediately repairs the segment] (aurora-storage-auto-repair-segment). AZ 1 to AZ 3 are labels.

sections.heading: The cluster volume grows by itself and you pay for used space

plan.problem: On a database server with its own disk, you choose the disk size in advance. You pay for empty space, and a full disk stops the database.
trace: **Nothing to size.** With Aurora you do not [provision either storage or I/O operations in advance] (aurora-pricing-storage-io-not-provisioned-in-advance).

**It grows with the data.** The cluster volume grows by itself as the [amount of data in your database increases] (aurora-cluster-volume-grows-automatically), from a [minimum of 10 GiB] (aurora-storage-grows-10-gib-to-256-tib-in-10-gib-increments).

**You pay for what is used.** You are [only charged for the space that you use] (aurora-charged-only-for-space-used); storage is [billed in per GB-month increments] (aurora-pricing-storage-billed-gb-month-both-configurations).

**Dropped data frees space.** When you drop or truncate a table, [the space allocated for that data is freed] (aurora-volume-shrinks-when-data-removed); this [automatic resizing when data is removed] (aurora-storage-features-depend-on-version) depends on the engine version.
plan.table: What the cluster volume does (columns: Event | Result): data grows | the volume grows; nobody resizes it; a table is dropped | space is freed (version-dependent); the volume reaches its maximum | the volume has a [maximum size of 256 tebibytes (TiB)] (aurora-cluster-volume-max-256-tib-overview), which varies by engine version; sorting large data sets | Aurora uses [separate local storage for nonpersistent, temporary files] (aurora-storage-separate-local-temp-files), not the volume. The 256 TiB value is volatile (changed in 2025): it can stand in this table, never in a question key.
plan.why: Why can Aurora bill only used space? The data sits on one [single, virtual volume] (aurora-cluster-volume-ssd-single-virtual) shared by every instance, so no instance owns a fixed disk. Compare RDS, where [Amazon RDS uses EBS volumes] (rds-storage-ebs-striping) that you allocate.
plan.exam_signal: "storage grows unpredictably" or "no capacity planning for database storage" points to the Aurora cluster volume, which grows as the [amount of data in your database increases] (aurora-cluster-volume-grows-automatically).
plan.body_extras: Reference only: maximum table size 64 TiB for Aurora MySQL and 32 TiB for Aurora PostgreSQL (aurora-table-size-limits-mysql-64-tib-postgresql-32-tib; B-list candidate, not planned); the 128 TiB to 256 TiB change is the alternate Changed recently entry (aurora-change-storage-max-256-tib); Limitless Database for data [beyond 256 TiB] (aurora-faq-limitless-beyond-256-tib): no sentence.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: Aurora storage grows with your data, and you pay for what you use. The thing to watch is the maximum, which depends on the version.
plan.stop_and_answer: A team plans to allocate 5 TB of storage for a new Aurora cluster that holds 300 GB today, to leave room for two years of growth. What do you tell them? Answer: there is nothing to allocate; you do not [provision either storage or I/O operations in advance] (aurora-pricing-storage-io-not-provisioned-in-advance), and you are [only charged for the space that you use] (aurora-charged-only-for-space-used). The sizes are example values.

sections.heading: Aurora Replicas read the shared volume, so replica lag stays low

plan.problem: An RDS read replica receives every change and writes it again to its own storage. Under heavy writes, that copy falls behind, and reads show old data.
trace: **The writer writes once.** The change lands in the shared cluster volume (subsection 2); no link needed for this step.

**Replicas read the same volume.** Aurora Replicas [connect to the same storage volume] (aurora-adding-replicas-read-same-volume-offload) as the primary DB instance but [support read operations only] (aurora-adding-replicas-read-same-volume-offload).
**Little to copy.** Because the volume is shared, [minimal additional work is required] (aurora-replicas-dedicated-reads-shared-volume-little-copy-work) to give each replica the data.

**Lag stays short.** Replica lag is usually [much less than 100 milliseconds] (aurora-replica-lag-under-100-ms); it [varies depending on the rate of database change] (aurora-replica-lag-varies-with-write-rate).
**Up to fifteen readers.** A cluster can have [up to 15 Aurora Replicas in addition to the primary DB instance] (aurora-replicas-up-to-15-in-addition-to-primary).
plan.table: RDS read replica or Aurora Replica (columns: Question | RDS read replica | Aurora Replica): How the data arrives | RDS [copies them asynchronously to the read replica] (rds-read-replica-async-read-only) | it reads the volume the writer wrote: replicas [share the same underlying storage] (aurora-cmp-replicas-share-storage-no-replica-writes); Storage | its own: [Amazon RDS uses EBS volumes] (rds-storage-ebs-striping) | none of its own; Typical lag | depends on the write load | [much less than 100 milliseconds] (aurora-replica-lag-under-100-ms); Failover target | [Can be manually promoted] (rds-compare-failover-vs-promote) | promoted automatically (subsection 6). Then the diagram aurora-replica-compare (caption and alt fixed in diagrams below; no numbered steps).
plan.diagram: aurora-replica-compare, after the table (caption and alt fixed in diagrams below; no numbered steps).
plan.why: Why does a shared volume cut lag? Replicas [share the same underlying storage] (aurora-cmp-replicas-share-storage-no-replica-writes) with the writer, so a replica writes no copy of the change; it reads the pages that the writer already stored. If the table already uses this display, link [work from the same underlying data] (aurora-mysql-replicas-same-underlying-data) only for Aurora MySQL, or write the reason without a second link.
plan.exam_signal: "read replicas fall behind at peak" or "scale reads with minimal replica lag" on MySQL or PostgreSQL points to Aurora Replicas, whose lag is usually [much less than 100 milliseconds] (aurora-replica-lag-under-100-ms); "reads must show every write at once" still points to the writer, because lag [varies depending on the rate of database change] (aurora-replica-lag-varies-with-write-rate). If the trace already uses both displays, link the second clause to [minimal replica lag] (aurora-replicas-return-same-data-minimal-lag).
plan.startup_example: > **Startup example:** Callvale's one read replica was up to 40 seconds behind at peak. Callvale now sends dashboard queries to two Aurora Replicas through the reader endpoint. (26 words; 40 is in uses_numbers; 'two' is a word.)
plan.body_extras: Reference only: a replica can use another instance class ([don't have to be of the same] (aurora-replicas-need-not-match-primary-instance-class)), but HA replicas should match (subsection 6); replicas have [two main purposes] (aurora-replicas-two-purposes-read-scale-availability); the FAQ says [tens of milliseconds] (aurora-faq-replica-lag-tens-of-ms-same-region) and the features page says single-digit milliseconds (aurora-cmp-replica-lag-often-single-digit-milliseconds): never put two lag figures in one sentence; the quota of 15 [15 read replicas] (aurora-quota-read-replicas-per-primary) cannot be raised for Aurora.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: Aurora Replicas read the writer's own volume, so they stay close behind. The thing to watch is lag: low, not zero.

sections.heading: The reader endpoint spreads connections, not single queries, across replicas

plan.problem: An application should not keep a list of DB instance names. Instances come and go, and the writer can change. Aurora gives the cluster a few stable names instead.
trace: **Writes go to the cluster endpoint.** It [connects to the current primary DB instance] (aurora-cluster-endpoint-connects-to-current-primary) and is [the only one that can perform write operations] (aurora-cluster-endpoint-only-one-for-writes).
**Reads go to the reader endpoint.** It gives [connection-balancing support for read-only connections] (aurora-reader-endpoint-connection-balancing-read-only).

**It balances each connection once.** The reader endpoint [balances connections to available Aurora Replicas] (aurora-reader-endpoint-balances-connections-not-queries) and [doesn't balance individual queries] (aurora-reader-endpoint-balances-connections-not-queries).

**No replica, no readers.** In a cluster with [no Aurora Replicas] (aurora-reader-endpoint-no-replica-goes-to-primary-writes-allowed), the [reader endpoint connects to the primary instance] (aurora-reader-endpoint-no-replica-goes-to-primary-writes-allowed).
plan.table: Four kinds of endpoint (columns: Endpoint | Connects to | Use it for): cluster | the current writer | the [cluster endpoint for read/write] (aurora-ha-use-cluster-and-reader-endpoints) work; reader | the Aurora Replicas | the [reader endpoint for read-only connections] (aurora-ha-use-cluster-and-reader-endpoints); custom | [a set of DB instances that you choose] (aurora-custom-endpoint-set-of-chosen-instances) | a group, such as large replicas for reports; instance | one DB instance: it [connects to a specific DB instance] (aurora-instance-endpoint-specific-db-instance) | to [diagnose capacity or performance issues] (aurora-instance-endpoint-use-diagnose-one-instance).
plan.why: Why balance connections and not queries? The choice of replica happens when a connection opens. To spread single queries, open a new [connection to the reader endpoint for each query] (aurora-reader-endpoint-new-connection-per-query-to-balance).
plan.exam_signal: "send read-only queries to the replicas, also to replicas added later, without changing the application" points to the reader endpoint ([connection-balancing support for read-only connections] (aurora-reader-endpoint-connection-balancing-read-only)); "reports must run only on the two largest replicas" points to a custom endpoint ([a set of DB instances that you choose] (aurora-custom-endpoint-set-of-chosen-instances)).
plan.exam_trap_text: > **Exam trap:** A connection pool on the reader endpoint does not spread each query. The endpoint [doesn't balance individual queries] (aurora-reader-endpoint-balances-connections-not-queries), so a long-lived connection keeps using the replica it first reached. <!-- trap: aurora-trap-reader-endpoint-balances-queries -->
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: custom endpoints (at most 70 words). A cluster has [no custom endpoints until you create one] (aurora-custom-endpoint-none-until-created-up-to-five). Members of a `READER` custom endpoint are [automatically adjusted during failovers and promotions] (aurora-custom-endpoint-reader-type-membership-follows-failover); an `ANY` endpoint can hold [Both reader and writer DB instances] (aurora-custom-endpoint-types-reader-any). With custom endpoints you [typically don't use the reader endpoint] (aurora-custom-endpoint-skip-reader-endpoint-when-using). If words remain: [Custom endpoints are not included in the snapshot] (aurora-custom-endpoint-not-in-snapshot-recreate-after-restore), so you [create them again after restoring] (aurora-custom-endpoint-not-in-snapshot-recreate-after-restore).
plan.body_extras: Reference only: the number of custom endpoints per cluster has two facts with different scopes (aurora-custom-endpoint-none-until-created-up-to-five says up to five and not adjustable in the guide; aurora-quota-custom-endpoints-per-cluster says 5 by default, adjustable through Service Quotas): write no number; the cluster and reader endpoints are built in and [can't create, delete, or modify] (aurora-cluster-endpoint-builtin-cannot-modify); the instance endpoint's location is in the console only (aurora-instance-endpoint-console-only).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: write through the cluster endpoint and read through the reader endpoint. The thing to watch is that the reader endpoint balances connections.
plan.stop_and_answer: A reporting job opens one connection to the reader endpoint at 08:00 and runs 5,000 queries on it until 18:00. The cluster has three Aurora Replicas. How many replicas serve those queries? Answer: one; the reader endpoint [balances connections to available Aurora Replicas] (aurora-reader-endpoint-balances-connections-not-queries), not queries. To spread them, open a new [connection to the reader endpoint for each query] (aurora-reader-endpoint-new-connection-per-query-to-balance). The times and counts are example values.

sections.heading: When the writer fails, Aurora promotes a replica behind the same endpoint

plan.problem: The writer DB instance can fail, and so can its Availability Zone. Writes must move to another DB instance by themselves, and the application must find it.
trace: **Aurora detects it.** Aurora [detects database problems] (aurora-detects-problems-activates-failover-automatically) and [activates the failover mechanism automatically] (aurora-detects-problems-activates-failover-automatically).
**A replica becomes the writer.** Aurora [automatically fails over to an Aurora Replica] (aurora-auto-failover-to-replica); the priority tier decides which one (Go deeper).
**The endpoint follows.** The cluster endpoint [stays the same even when a failover promotes] (aurora-cluster-endpoint-stays-same-after-failover) a new writer.

**A short break.** During the switch, [read and write operations fail with an exception] (aurora-failover-read-write-fail-with-exception); service is typically back in [less than 60 seconds] (aurora-failover-time-with-replica-guide), often in [less than 30 seconds] (aurora-failover-time-with-replica-guide).
plan.table: When the writer fails (columns: Cluster | What Aurora does | Typical time): a writer and a replica in another AZ | [promoting an existing Aurora Replica] (aurora-failover-new-primary-by-promoting-or-creating) | [less than 60 seconds] (aurora-failover-time-with-replica-guide); one DB instance only | the primary is [recreated in the same AZ] (aurora-no-replica-primary-recreated-same-az) | [less than 10 minutes] (aurora-failover-time-without-replica); all instances in one AZ, and that AZ fails | you [manually create one or more new DB instances] (aurora-single-az-cluster-create-instances-manually) in another AZ | until you act.
plan.why: Why keep a replica of the same size in another zone? [Promoting an Aurora Replica] (aurora-promoting-replica-faster-than-new-primary) is [much faster than creating a new primary instance] (aurora-promoting-replica-faster-than-new-primary), so AWS advises replicas of the [same DB instance class as the primary instance] (aurora-replica-recommend-same-class-different-az) placed [in different Availability Zones] (aurora-replica-recommend-same-class-different-az).
plan.exam_signal: "fail over automatically within a minute if the writer or its Availability Zone fails" points to an Aurora Replica in another AZ: Aurora [automatically fails over to an Aurora Replica] (aurora-auto-failover-to-replica); "the connection string must not change after a failover" points to the cluster endpoint ([connect to the cluster endpoint] (aurora-cluster-endpoint-stays-same-after-failover)).
plan.spot_the_bug: **Spot the bug.** A production Aurora cluster has one writer and two Aurora Replicas. To keep traffic between them fast, the team placed all three DB instances in AZ 1. 'The storage is in three zones anyway,' they say. What is wrong? Reveal (about 55 words): the data survives an AZ 1 outage, but no DB instance does; no replica in another zone can be promoted, so you must [manually create one or more new DB instances] (aurora-single-az-cluster-create-instances-manually). Place replicas [in different Availability Zones] (aurora-replica-recommend-same-class-different-az). AZ 1 is a label.
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: which replica wins, and faster reconnects (at most 70 words). Priorities run from [0 for the highest priority to 15 for the lowest priority] (aurora-promotion-priority-range); on a tie, RDS promotes [the replica that is largest in size] (aurora-promotion-tie-break-largest). A low tier is not a lock: RDS [will promote the lower priority replica] (aurora-faq-low-priority-replica-still-promoted-if-needed) when the others are unhealthy. RDS Proxy cuts failover time by [up to 66%] (aurora-rds-proxy-failover-reduction-66-percent). Cut the proxy sentence first if over 70 words.
plan.body_extras: Reference only: the FAQ says failover typically completes [within 30 seconds] (aurora-faq-failover-cname-within-30s): never two failover-time links in one sentence; test failovers ([Test failover for your DB cluster] (aurora-best-practice-test-failover)); a client DNS cache under 30 seconds (aurora-best-practice-dns-ttl-under-30-seconds; B-list candidate); Aurora PostgreSQL cluster cache management keeps a warm cache on a chosen reader (aurora-postgres-cluster-cache-mgmt-preserves-cache); the reader endpoint can point at the new writer [for a short time] (aurora-reader-endpoint-may-point-to-new-primary-briefly); convert a single-AZ cluster by [adding a new reader DB instance] (aurora-convert-to-multi-az-by-adding-reader-other-az).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: Aurora promotes a replica, and the cluster endpoint follows it. The thing to watch is where your replicas run.
plan.stop_and_answer: A cluster has its writer in AZ 1 and one Aurora Replica in AZ 2. The application connects with the instance endpoint of the writer. After a failover, writes keep failing although the replica is now the writer. Why? Answer: an instance endpoint [connects to a specific DB instance] (aurora-instance-endpoint-specific-db-instance); only the writer and reader endpoints [automatically change which DB instance they connect] (aurora-writer-reader-endpoints-follow-failover-instance-endpoints-not) to. Use the cluster endpoint.

sections.heading: Aurora Auto Scaling adds and removes Aurora Replicas for read load

plan.problem: Read traffic rises every morning and falls at night. A fixed number of replicas is too small at the peak and wasted at night.
trace: **Set a range.** The scaling policy sets the [minimum and maximum number of Aurora Replicas] (aurora-auto-scaling-policy-min-max-replicas), each between [0–15] (aurora-autoscaling-replica-count-range).

**Track one metric.** Target tracking [creates and manages CloudWatch alarms] (aurora-auto-scaling-target-tracking-cloudwatch) for a metric such as average replica CPU, [RDSReaderAverageCPUUtilization] (aurora-autoscaling-predefined-metric-reader-cpu).

**Add and remove replicas.** Aurora Auto Scaling [dynamically adjusts the number of Aurora Replicas] (aurora-cmp-aurora-auto-scaling-adjusts-replicas); a new replica has the [same DB instance class] (aurora-auto-scaling-new-replica-same-class-as-primary) as the primary.
**Applications find them.** Applications must [support connections to new Aurora Replicas] (aurora-auto-scaling-use-reader-endpoint); AWS advises the reader endpoint for that.
plan.table: What Aurora Auto Scaling changes (columns: Workload | Does it scale?): reads on the replicas | yes: it helps [only on the reader instances] (aurora-autoscaling-writer-not-scaled); writes on the writer | no (same fact, linked once in row 1); replicas that you added by hand | it [only removes Aurora Replicas that it created] (aurora-autoscaling-removes-only-own-replicas); Aurora Serverless v2 readers | no: [Aurora Auto Scaling isn't supported] (aurora-serverless-not-supported-with-aurora-auto-scaling).
plan.why: Why only readers? A cluster has [one primary DB instance] (aurora-one-primary-per-cluster), so more instances can only add read capacity. A busy writer needs a larger instance class instead (the [Apply Immediately flag] (aurora-faq-compute-scaling-manual) changes it now; otherwise the change waits for the maintenance window).
plan.exam_signal: "read traffic varies during the day" with provisioned instances points to Aurora Auto Scaling ([dynamically adjusts the number of Aurora Replicas] (aurora-cmp-aurora-auto-scaling-adjusts-replicas)); "the writer's CPU is high from writes" does not, because it scales [only on the reader instances] (aurora-autoscaling-writer-not-scaled).
plan.exam_trap_text: > **Exam trap:** Aurora Auto Scaling does not add write capacity. It helps [only on the reader instances] (aurora-autoscaling-writer-not-scaled); for a busy writer, choose a larger instance class or Aurora Serverless v2 (subsection 8). <!-- trap: aurora-trap-auto-scaling-scales-writer -->
plan.body_extras: Reference only: cooldowns default to [300 seconds] (aurora-auto-scaling-cooldown-default); a new replica gets the [last priority, which is 15 by default] (aurora-auto-scaling-new-replica-last-promotion-priority); it scales only when [all cluster instances are in the available state] (aurora-autoscaling-needs-all-instances-available); not for Global Database secondaries (aurora-autoscaling-global-secondary-unsupported); with Aurora Serverless v2, create readers in advance and [leave them scaled down to low capacity] (aurora-serverless-readers-alternative-to-aurora-auto-scaling).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: Aurora Auto Scaling adds replicas when reads grow and removes them later. The thing to watch is the writer: it keeps its size.
plan.stop_and_answer: A team created two Aurora Replicas by hand. At the morning peak, Aurora Auto Scaling added three more. At night the load drops. Can Aurora Auto Scaling remove the team's two replicas? Answer: no; it [only removes Aurora Replicas that it created] (aurora-autoscaling-removes-only-own-replicas). The counts are example values.

sections.heading: Aurora Serverless v2 changes capacity with load inside a range you set

plan.problem: A provisioned DB instance has a fixed size. When load is hard to predict, you pay for capacity that waits idle, or you run short at the peak.
trace: **Choose the instance class db.serverless.** It is a [special DB instance class type] (aurora-serverless-db-serverless-instance-class-type) inside an ordinary Aurora cluster.

**Set a range in ACUs.** Each Aurora capacity unit (ACU) has [approximately 2 gibibytes (GiB) of memory] (aurora-serverless-acu-about-2-gib-memory) with matching CPU and networking; you [specify the minimum and maximum capacity range] (aurora-serverless-specify-min-max-capacity-range).

**Aurora follows the load.** It [continuously tracks] (aurora-serverless-scales-up-on-cpu-memory-network-load) [CPU, memory, and network] (aurora-serverless-scales-up-on-cpu-memory-network-load) and scales in [increments as small as 0.5 ACUs] (aurora-serverless-scaling-increments-as-small-as-half-acu).
**No quiet moment needed.** Scaling happens while connections are open: Aurora [doesn't wait for a quiet point] (aurora-serverless-scaling-with-open-connections-no-quiet-point).

**You pay for what runs.** Charges are [measured in terms of ACU-hours] (aurora-serverless-billing-unit-acu-hours), at [a flat rate per second of ACU usage] (aurora-serverless-faq-billed-per-second-acu).
plan.table: Does the instance pause when idle? (columns: Setting | Result): minimum capacity zero ACUs, no connections | it can [pause after a period with no user connections] (aurora-serverless-auto-pause-after-no-connections); minimum capacity [higher than zero ACUs] (aurora-serverless-min-capacity-above-zero-no-pause) | it does not pause; minimum zero, but RDS Proxy in front | it [won't automatically pause] (aurora-serverless-rds-proxy-blocks-auto-pause); a paused instance gets a connection | it [automatically resumes and accepts the connection] (aurora-serverless-connect-to-paused-instance-resumes). Write 'zero ACUs' in words in the cells (no digit outside a link).
plan.why: Why not a bigger provisioned instance? With fixed capacity you can face [higher costs if you overprovision] (aurora-serverless-overprovision-raises-cost); AWS says Aurora Serverless v2 is intended for [variable or "spiky" workloads] (aurora-serverless-choose-variable-spiky-workloads).
plan.exam_signal: "unpredictable", "spiky" or "used a few hours a day" points to Aurora Serverless v2 ([variable or "spiky" workloads] (aurora-serverless-choose-variable-spiky-workloads)); "steady load around the clock" points to provisioned instances, which are [suitable for steady workloads] (aurora-serverless-provisioned-suited-to-steady-workloads). If the Why already links the spiky display, link [development and test systems] (aurora-serverless-choose-multitenant-dev-test) here for the first clause instead.
plan.exam_trap_text: > **Exam trap:** Idle does not mean free. The instances can pause only when you set the minimum capacity [for the cluster to zero ACUs] (aurora-serverless-auto-pause-min-capacity-zero), and even then storage is charged: only the [instance charge is zero] (aurora-serverless-auto-pause-billing-storage-still-charged). <!-- trap: aurora-trap-serverless-pauses-whenever-idle -->
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence: one cluster can mix [both Aurora serverless and provisioned capacity] (aurora-serverless-mixed-configuration-cluster). Reference only: the range 0 to 256 ACUs (aurora-serverless-capacity-range-0-256-acu-half-acu-steps: volatile, B-list); scaling to zero is new since 2024 (aurora-serverless-change-scale-to-zero: Changed recently entry); resume in [approximately 15 seconds] (aurora-serverless-auto-pause-resume-about-15-seconds: B-list); readers in tiers 0 and 1 follow the writer (aurora-serverless-tier-0-1-readers-follow-writer); convert a provisioned writer by failover (aurora-serverless-convert-writer-via-failover); it [works like provisioned for failover] (aurora-serverless-works-like-provisioned-for-failover); the Data API is an [HTTP-based API] (aurora-faq-data-api-http-no-drivers-no-pools-no-vpc) for new Lambda-based applications (FAQ only); the 90% savings claim (aurora-serverless-product-save-up-to-90-percent) is marketing: no sentence. Aurora Serverless v1 appears at most once (see naming).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: Aurora Serverless v2 grows and shrinks the instance with the load. The thing to watch is the minimum capacity you set.
plan.stop_and_answer: A team sets the minimum and the maximum capacity of an Aurora Serverless v2 cluster to the same value, 16 ACUs, to make costs predictable. At the next sales peak, queries slow down. Will Aurora add capacity? Answer: no; with [identical] (aurora-serverless-identical-min-max-never-scales) minimum and maximum, [the capacity never scales up or down] (aurora-serverless-identical-min-max-never-scales). 16 ACUs is an example value.

sections.heading: Aurora Global Database copies the cluster volume to read-only Regions

plan.problem: A whole Region can fail, and users far from it wait for every read. A copy in another Region must stay current without slowing the writer, because [AWS Regions are isolated from each other] (aurora-resources-not-auto-replicated-across-regions).
trace: **One primary Region writes.** [Only the primary cluster performs write operations] (aurora-global-db-only-primary-writes).

**Storage ships the changes.** Replication uses the [cluster storage volume and not the database engine] (aurora-global-db-replication-uses-storage-not-engine), with latency [typically under a second] (aurora-global-replication-latency-under-1-second).

**Secondary Regions read.** A secondary Region runs a cluster [made up entirely of Aurora Replicas] (aurora-global-db-secondary-region-readers-only); applications there [connect to the reader endpoint] (aurora-global-db-scale-reads-connect-to-nearby-reader-endpoint) in their own Region.
**Several Regions.** A global database can have [up to 10 secondary AWS Regions] (aurora-global-secondary-regions-max-10); the value changed in 2025 (Changed recently), so no question turns on it.
plan.table: Ways to copy Aurora data to another Region (columns: Question | Aurora Global Database | Aurora MySQL binlog replica | Snapshot copy): How it copies | [storage-based replication] (aurora-global-db-product-page-storage-based-replication-dedicated) | [MySQL binary log (binlog) replication] (aurora-mysql-binlog-cross-region-replica-up-to-five) | you [manually copy Aurora snapshots] (aurora-no-cross-region-automated-backup-replication); Typical lag | [typically under a second] (aurora-global-replication-latency-under-1-second) | [there is more lag time] (aurora-cmp-binlog-cross-region-replica-more-lag) | the time since the last copy; Engines | [both Aurora MySQL and Aurora PostgreSQL] (aurora-faq-global-db-both-engines) | Aurora MySQL only | both. Four columns; cells at most 15 words.
plan.why: Why replicate in storage? The writer does no extra work: the replication has [little performance impact on the primary DB cluster] (aurora-global-db-replication-little-primary-performance-impact), and you [don't need to configure or manage] (aurora-global-db-no-binlog-management) binlog replication.
plan.exam_signal: "recover from a Regional outage with an RPO of seconds" or "low-latency reads for users around the world" on a relational database points to Aurora Global Database, built for [low latency global reads and disaster recovery] (aurora-global-database-multi-region-ha); "every Region must accept writes" points to DynamoDB global tables, where [Any global table replica] (dynamodb-global-table-any-replica-serves-reads-writes) can [serve reads and writes] (dynamodb-global-table-any-replica-serves-reads-writes).
plan.exam_trap_text: > **Exam trap:** Aurora PostgreSQL has no cross-Region read replica like the Aurora MySQL binlog replica. Aurora PostgreSQL [doesn't support cross-Region Aurora Replicas] (aurora-postgres-no-cross-region-aurora-replicas); use Aurora Global Database. <!-- trap: aurora-trap-postgres-cross-region-replica -->
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: write forwarding (at most 70 words). Secondary clusters can [forward SQL statements that perform write operations] (aurora-write-forwarding-secondary-forward-sql-writes) to the primary; [write forwarding isn't enabled] (aurora-write-forwarding-off-by-default-secondary) when you add a secondary. The data is [always changed first on the primary cluster] (aurora-write-forwarding-primary-source-of-truth). It suits [occasional DML statements] (aurora-global-db-occasional-writes-use-secondary-reader-with-write-forwarding), and it [doesn't support certain MySQL or PostgreSQL operations] (aurora-global-db-write-forwarding-unsupported-operations), such as DDL.
plan.body_extras: Reference only: between Regions you [pay for replicated write I/O operations] (aurora-pricing-global-db-replicated-write-io-between-regions); a secondary without DB instances is [not charged for compute, only for storage] (aurora-global-headless-secondary-no-compute-charge) and needs an instance before promotion (aurora-global-headless-needs-instance-before-promotion); a secondary can hold [up to 16 read-only DB instances] (aurora-global-secondary-cluster-max-16-reader-instances: B-list); memory-optimized classes (aurora-global-requires-memory-optimized-instance-class); Aurora Serverless v2 in secondaries (aurora-serverless-global-secondary-can-use-serverless); the FAQ's choice [either physical or logical replication] (aurora-faq-cross-region-physical-or-logical) is an FAQ item; the Secrets Manager restriction (aurora-global-db-secrets-manager-not-supported) is volatile: no sentence.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: Global Database copies the storage to other Regions in about a second. The thing to watch is writes: one Region takes them.
plan.stop_and_answer: A company runs Aurora PostgreSQL in us-east-1 and opens an office in Europe. Reports there are slow, and every write can stay in us-east-1. What gives the European office fast reads? Answer: an Aurora global database with a secondary cluster in a European Region; the office applications [connect to the reader endpoint] (aurora-global-db-scale-reads-connect-to-nearby-reader-endpoint) of that cluster.

sections.heading: A secondary Region takes over by failover after an outage, by switchover when healthy

plan.problem: Two events move the primary role to another Region: a planned move while everything is healthy, and an outage of the primary Region. Each needs its own operation.
trace: **Outage: fail over.** Use failover to [recover from an unplanned outage] (aurora-global-db-failover-use-for-unplanned-outage); AWS says the managed failover [method is recommended for disaster recovery] (aurora-global-db-managed-failover-recommended-for-dr).

**Failover does not wait.** Managed failover [doesn't wait for data to synchronize] (aurora-global-db-managed-failover-no-wait-async), so the RPO is typically a [non-zero value measured in seconds] (aurora-global-failover-rpo-nonzero-seconds); the chosen secondary typically takes the primary role [within a few minutes] (aurora-global-managed-failover-primary-role-few-minutes).

**Planned move: switch over.** A switchover lets you [relocate the primary cluster] (aurora-global-db-switchover-planned-no-data-loss) [with no data loss] (aurora-global-db-switchover-planned-no-data-loss), because Aurora first [waits for the target secondary Region clusters] (aurora-global-db-switchover-waits-for-sync) to catch up.

**One name for writes.** The global writer endpoint [always points to the current writer DB instance] (aurora-global-db-global-writer-single-readwrite-endpoint), so you [don't need to change the connection settings] (aurora-global-db-writer-endpoint-no-app-change-after-switchover) after a switchover.
plan.table: Failover or switchover (columns: Question | Failover | Switchover): When to use it | to [recover from an unplanned outage] (aurora-global-db-failover-use-for-unplanned-outage) | for [controlled scenarios, such as operational maintenance] (aurora-global-db-switchover-controlled-scenarios); State of the clusters | the primary Region has failed | all [in a healthy state] (aurora-global-db-switchover-healthy-only-unplanned-use-failover); Data loss | possible: unreplicated writes are lost | [RPO is 0 (no data loss)] (aurora-global-switchover-rpo-zero); The old primary | Aurora [automatically adds back the old primary Region] (aurora-global-db-managed-failover-readds-old-primary) | the topology is kept ([maintains your global database's existing replication topology] (aurora-global-db-switchover-keeps-topology)).
plan.why: Why can a failover lose data? Aurora [asynchronously replicates all data and updates] (aurora-global-database-async-replication-secondary) to the secondaries, so the newest writes can still be on their way when the primary Region fails.
plan.exam_signal: "the primary Region is unavailable; restore write access in the secondary Region" points to a managed cross-Region failover ([method is recommended for disaster recovery] (aurora-global-db-managed-failover-recommended-for-dr)); "planned maintenance; move the primary to another Region with no data loss" points to a switchover ([with no data loss] (aurora-global-db-switchover-planned-no-data-loss)). If the trace already uses both displays, link [controlled scenarios, such as operational maintenance] (aurora-global-db-switchover-controlled-scenarios) for the second clause.
plan.exam_trap_text: > **Exam trap:** A Global Database failover is not lossless. [Both failover methods can result] (aurora-global-db-failover-can-lose-writes-consistent-state) in a [loss of write transaction data that wasn't replicated] (aurora-global-db-failover-can-lose-writes-consistent-state); only a switchover of healthy clusters has [RPO is 0 (no data loss)] (aurora-global-switchover-rpo-zero). <!-- trap: aurora-trap-global-failover-no-data-loss -->
plan.try_it: aurora-t02, after the table: one sentence ('Set an upper bound on the data loss of an Aurora PostgreSQL global database in a cluster parameter group, and watch AWS refuse a value that is too low.'), then 'See [3-do.md](3-do.md). <!-- task: aurora-t02 -->'.
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence: for Aurora PostgreSQL you can [manage the recovery point objective (RPO)] (aurora-global-db-postgres-rpo-managed-by-parameter) with a cluster parameter; when every secondary falls behind, [Aurora pauses transactions on the primary cluster] (aurora-global-db-rpo-blocks-commits-when-all-secondaries-behind). Reference only: AWS marketing and the FAQ say promotion in [less than 1 minute] (aurora-global-promote-secondary-under-1-minute) while the guide says RTO [in the order of minutes] (aurora-global-rto-order-of-minutes-guide): never in one sentence; fail back with a switchover (aurora-global-db-failback-via-switchover); a switchover takes [typically under 30 seconds] (aurora-global-switchover-time-typically-under-30-seconds: volatile, no sentence); manual failover by detaching a secondary (aurora-global-db-detach-secondary-standalone-readwrite); write fencing is best effort (aurora-global-db-write-fencing-best-effort-split-brain); DR strategies of the whitepaper belong to chapter 40.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: fail over after an outage, switch over when all is healthy. The thing to watch is data loss: a failover can lose seconds.
plan.stop_and_answer: A bank requires an RPO of 15 minutes and an RTO of 1 hour if the primary Region is lost. On paper, does Aurora Global Database meet both? Answer: yes on paper: a failover loses a [non-zero value measured in seconds] (aurora-global-failover-rpo-nonzero-seconds) of writes, and the secondary takes the primary role [within a few minutes] (aurora-global-managed-failover-primary-role-few-minutes); only a recovery test proves it. The 15 minutes and 1 hour are example values in the prompt.

sections.heading: Backups are continuous, and every restore creates a new cluster

plan.problem: A faulty release deletes rows at 14:05. The team needs the data as it was at 14:04, and it must also keep month-end copies for years.
trace: **Backups run all the time.** Aurora [backs up your cluster volume automatically] (aurora-backups-automatic-continuous-incremental); the backups are [continuous and incremental] (aurora-backup-continuous-incremental-no-impact), and you [can't disable automated backups on Aurora] (aurora-backup-cannot-disable-automated).
**You choose how long.** The retention period is [1–35 days] (aurora-backup-retention-period-range-1-35-days).

**Restore to a second.** Point-in-time recovery reaches [any second during your retention period] (aurora-pitr-any-second-within-retention-period); the latest restorable time is typically [within 5 minutes of the current time] (aurora-backup-latest-restorable-time-within-5-minutes).

**A restore is a new cluster.** A point-in-time restore means [creating a new DB cluster] (aurora-pitr-creates-new-cluster); from a snapshot, too, [a new DB cluster is created] (aurora-restore-always-creates-new-cluster).
plan.table: Four ways back in time (columns: Need | Tool | Result): data from three days ago | point-in-time restore | a new cluster (linked in the trace); a copy kept for years | a manual snapshot: [snapshots don't expire] (aurora-snapshots-do-not-expire) | a new cluster when you restore it; a test copy of production today | a clone that [shares the same data pages as the original] (aurora-clone-shares-data-pages-separate-volume) | a separate volume; rewind Aurora MySQL by minutes | Backtrack, which [rewinds the DB cluster in minutes] (aurora-backtrack-in-minutes-no-new-cluster) | the same cluster.
plan.why: Why is a restore a new cluster? The running cluster stays untouched while you check the restored data; then you copy rows back or move the application. To keep data longer than the retention period, [copy it to create a manual snapshot] (aurora-automated-backup-copy-to-keep-longer).
plan.exam_signal: "restore the database to its state of 10 minutes ago" points to point-in-time recovery to a new cluster ([any second during your retention period] (aurora-pitr-any-second-within-retention-period)); "retain backups for 7 years" points to manual snapshots, because [snapshots don't expire] (aurora-snapshots-do-not-expire), or to an export to Amazon S3 for [very long-term backups] (aurora-export-snapshot-to-s3-for-long-term). If the table uses the snapshot display, keep only the export link here.
plan.exam_trap_text: > **Exam trap:** A point-in-time restore does not roll back the running cluster: it means [creating a new DB cluster] (aurora-pitr-creates-new-cluster). Backtrack rewinds in place, but only on Aurora MySQL clusters [created with the Backtrack feature enabled] (aurora-backtrack-only-if-enabled-at-creation). <!-- trap: aurora-trap-restore-in-place -->
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: Backtrack and clones (at most 70 words). [Backtrack is not available for Aurora PostgreSQL] (aurora-backtrack-not-for-postgresql); its window has a limit of [72 hours] (aurora-backtrack-window-limit-72-hours), and [Backtracking affects the entire DB cluster] (aurora-backtrack-whole-cluster-not-single-table). It is [not a replacement for backing up] (aurora-backtrack-rewinds-not-replacement-for-backups). A clone stores only changes: storage is [allocated only when changes are made to data] (aurora-clone-copy-on-write-storage-on-change).
plan.body_extras: Reference only: the default retention is [one day] (aurora-backup-retention-default-1-day: B-list); you can retain automated backups when you delete a cluster (aurora-retain-automated-backups-after-delete), but [a final snapshot doesn't expire] (aurora-final-snapshot-does-not-expire-retained-backups-do); deletion protection is on by default only in the console (aurora-deletion-protection-default-console-vs-cli); AWS Backup can manage Aurora backups (aurora-aws-backup-manages-clusters; chapter 24); cross-Region copies are manual snapshot copies (subsection 9 table); sharing: up to 20 accounts, same Region, not with the default KMS key (aurora-snapshot-share-up-to-20-accounts, aurora-faq-shared-snapshot-same-region-only, aurora-snapshot-default-kms-key-cannot-be-shared); exports are Parquet (aurora-export-snapshot-parquet-format); backup storage up to the cluster size is free (aurora-backup-storage-free-up-to-total-storage).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: Aurora backs up all the time, and a restore gives you a new cluster. The thing to watch is the retention period you set.
plan.stop_and_answer: A company must keep a restorable copy of its month-end data for 7 years. It sets the backup retention period to the highest value. Is that enough? Answer: no; the retention period is [1–35 days] (aurora-backup-retention-period-range-1-35-days). Take a manual snapshot at each month-end, because [snapshots don't expire] (aurora-snapshots-do-not-expire). 7 years is an example value.

sections.heading: Aurora Standard charges for each I/O, and I/O-Optimized includes it

plan.problem: Aurora bills DB instances and storage and, in one configuration, every I/O request. An I/O-heavy workload can see a large I/O bill that changes every month.
trace: **Standard: pay per request.** With Aurora Standard you pay a [standard rate per 1 million requests for I/O operations] (aurora-standard-pays-per-million-io) on top of instances and storage.

**I/O-Optimized: I/O included.** With Aurora I/O-Optimized you [pay only for the usage and storage] (aurora-io-optimized-no-io-charges), with [no additional charges for read and write I/O] (aurora-io-optimized-no-io-charges).

**Choose by the I/O share.** I/O-Optimized is the best choice when I/O is [25% or more] (aurora-io-optimized-best-when-io-25-percent-or-more) of your Aurora spending; Standard is best below that ([less than 25%] (aurora-standard-best-when-io-under-25-percent)).

**Switching has limits.** You can move to I/O-Optimized [once every 30 days] (aurora-io-switch-standard-to-io-optimized-once-every-30-days), and back to Standard [at any time] (aurora-io-switch-io-optimized-to-standard-any-time).
plan.table: Standard or I/O-Optimized (columns: Question | Aurora Standard | Aurora I/O-Optimized): I/O charges | [you pay per-request for I/O] (aurora-faq-standard-pay-per-io-vs-io-optimized-included) | [included at no additional charge] (aurora-faq-standard-pay-per-io-vs-io-optimized-included); Reserved Instances cover I/O | no | yes: I/O costs are [only covered when your database cluster is configured] (aurora-pricing-reserved-instances-io-only-with-io-optimized) as I/O-Optimized; Readers and writers | I/O is [counted the same way] (aurora-io-counted-same-writer-reader) on every DB instance | no I/O bill at all.
plan.why: Why two models? For light I/O, paying per request is cheapest; for heavy I/O, AWS cites [improved price performance for I/O-intensive applications] (aurora-faq-io-optimized-fits-io-intensive-workloads) and a predictable bill.
plan.exam_signal: "I/O-intensive" or "unpredictable I/O costs" points to Aurora I/O-Optimized ([no additional charges for read and write I/O] (aurora-io-optimized-no-io-charges)); "low I/O, cost-sensitive" points to Aurora Standard. Link the second clause only if the trace has not used [less than 25%] (aurora-standard-best-when-io-under-25-percent).
plan.exam_trap_text: > **Exam trap:** I/O-Optimized does not always cost less. It is the best choice at [25% or more] (aurora-io-optimized-best-when-io-25-percent-or-more) of spending on I/O; below that share, Aurora Standard is the cheaper choice. <!-- trap: aurora-trap-io-optimized-always-cheaper -->
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence: a steady cluster saves with Reserved Instances, which are [appropriate for steady-state database workloads] (aurora-pricing-reserved-instances-steady-state). Reference only: stop a cluster for [up to seven days] (aurora-stop-cluster-up-to-seven-days: B-list) and pay storage but no instance hours (aurora-stopped-cluster-charges-storage-not-instance-hours); On-Demand billing per second with a [10-minute minimum charge] (aurora-on-demand-billing-one-second-increments-ten-minute-minimum); up to 40% savings above the 25% share (aurora-io-optimized-save-up-to-40-percent-above-25-percent-io); Database Savings Plans (volatile; chapter 41); RDS Extended Support (volatile; reference only); EC2 to Aurora data transfer is free in one AZ (aurora-pricing-data-transfer-same-az-ec2-free).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: Standard bills each I/O request, and I/O-Optimized has no I/O charges. The thing to watch is the I/O share of your bill.
plan.stop_and_answer: A cluster's Aurora bill is 40% I/O charges, and the team moved it to I/O-Optimized 10 days ago. Now they want to move back to Standard for a week and then return to I/O-Optimized. Can they? Answer: they can move back to Standard [at any time] (aurora-io-switch-io-optimized-to-standard-any-time), but the return to I/O-Optimized must wait: the move is allowed [once every 30 days] (aurora-io-switch-standard-to-io-optimized-once-every-30-days). The percentages and days are example values.

sections.heading: Data moves into Aurora by snapshot, by Aurora read replica or by AWS DMS

plan.problem: A database already runs on Amazon RDS, on premises, or on another engine. The move must copy the data and switch the application with as little downtime as the business accepts.
trace: **Same engine from RDS: a snapshot.** You can migrate [from an RDS for PostgreSQL DB snapshot] (aurora-postgres-migrate-snapshot-from-rds) to an Aurora PostgreSQL cluster; for MySQL, snapshot migrations [typically complete in under an hour] (aurora-mysql-migrate-from-rds-snapshot-under-an-hour).

**Same engine, short cutover: an Aurora read replica.** Aurora can build an Aurora read replica of the RDS DB instance for [migration to Aurora PostgreSQL] (aurora-rds-postgres-read-replica-for-migration), only [within the same AWS Region and account] (aurora-postgres-read-replica-migration-same-region-account); it can take [several hours per terabyte of data] (aurora-postgres-migrate-replica-hours-per-terabyte).

**Cut over at zero lag.** [Stop all database write workload on the source] (aurora-postgres-promote-stop-write-workload-on-source); when the lag is zero, [you can stop replication] (aurora-postgres-migrate-replica-lag-zero-stop-replication) and the replica becomes a standalone cluster.

**Another engine: convert, then copy.** From Oracle or SQL Server, AWS suggests the [AWS Schema Conversion Tool (AWS SCT)] (aurora-migrate-heterogeneous-consider-sct) for the schema and [AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS)] (aurora-postgres-non-postgres-source-use-dms) for the data.
plan.table: Which path (columns: Source | Path): RDS for MySQL or PostgreSQL, a maintenance window is fine | snapshot migration ([creating and restoring snapshots] (aurora-migrate-from-rds-snapshot-or-replication)); RDS for MySQL or PostgreSQL, short cutover | Aurora read replica, then promote ([setting up one-way replication] (aurora-migrate-from-rds-snapshot-or-replication)); MySQL outside RDS | binlog replication from [an external MySQL database] (aurora-mysql-binlog-replication-external-mysql-inside-or-outside-aws); Oracle or SQL Server | AWS SCT, then AWS DMS (chapter 39 owns both tools). Two columns; no downtime figures: no fact gives them.
plan.why: Why an Aurora read replica for the move? The source keeps serving while the copy catches up, so the switch waits only for the last changes; AWS uses this replica for migration [rather than for ongoing replication] (aurora-rds-postgres-read-replica-for-migration).
plan.exam_signal: "migrate RDS for PostgreSQL to Aurora with minimal downtime" points to an Aurora read replica, then promotion ([migration to Aurora PostgreSQL] (aurora-rds-postgres-read-replica-for-migration)); "migrate Oracle to Aurora PostgreSQL" points to AWS SCT and AWS DMS ([AWS Schema Conversion Tool (AWS SCT)] (aurora-migrate-heterogeneous-consider-sct)). If the trace uses both displays, link [different underlying engine than Aurora's] (aurora-migrate-heterogeneous-consider-sct) in the second clause.
plan.spot_the_bug: **Spot the bug.** A team moves RDS for PostgreSQL to Aurora with an Aurora read replica. To save time, it promotes the replica at 09:00 while the application still writes to the RDS DB instance, and points the application at Aurora at 09:30. What is wrong? Reveal (about 50 words): the writes from 09:00 to 09:30 stay on RDS, because after promotion the two databases [are unlinked] (aurora-postgres-promotion-unlinks-source). [Stop all database write workload on the source] (aurora-postgres-promote-stop-write-workload-on-source) first, and promote when the lag of the [Aurora PostgreSQL read replica is zero] (aurora-postgres-migrate-replica-lag-zero-stop-replication).
plan.body_extras: Reference only: one Aurora read replica per RDS for MySQL DB instance (aurora-mysql-only-one-aurora-read-replica-per-rds-mysql); standard tools work ([Standard MySQL import and export tools] (aurora-mysql-standard-import-export-tools-work)); Aurora PostgreSQL can import from Amazon S3 (aurora-postgres-import-from-s3); Babelfish for SQL Server applications (aurora-faq-babelfish-sql-server: FAQ only); logical replication of single tables (aurora-postgres-logical-replication-individual-tables).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: from RDS, promote an Aurora read replica. The thing to watch is stopping writes before the cutover.
plan.stop_and_answer: A company wants to move a 2 TB RDS for PostgreSQL database into Aurora PostgreSQL in a different AWS account, with a short cutover. Can it use an Aurora read replica? Answer: no; that option works only [within the same AWS Region and account] (aurora-postgres-read-replica-migration-same-region-account). It needs another path, for example a snapshot. 2 TB is an example value.

sections.heading: Encryption at rest is set at creation and covers the whole cluster

plan.problem: A security review asks two questions: is the data encrypted on disk, in every backup and replica, and is it encrypted on the network?
trace: **One key for the cluster.** Aurora [uses an AWS Key Management Service key] (aurora-encryption-uses-aws-kms-key); every DB instance shares storage [encrypted with the same KMS key] (aurora-encryption-same-kms-key-all-instances).
**Every copy follows.** In an encrypted cluster, the instances and the [logs, backups, and snapshots are encrypted] (aurora-encrypted-cluster-all-instances-logs-backups-snapshots).

**Existing clusters: restore, not modify.** You [can't convert an unencrypted DB cluster] (aurora-encryption-cannot-convert-unencrypted-in-place) to an encrypted one, but you can [restore an unencrypted snapshot] (aurora-encryption-cannot-convert-unencrypted-in-place) to an encrypted cluster if you [specify a KMS key when you restore] (aurora-restore-unencrypted-snapshot-specify-kms-key).

**On the network: TLS.** Clients can [encrypt a connection to a DB cluster] (aurora-ssl-tls-connections-both-engines) with TLS; Aurora PostgreSQL requires it through the `rds.force_ssl` parameter ([use `rds.force_ssl` parameter] (aurora-postgres-rds-force-ssl-parameter)), Aurora MySQL through the [`require_secure_transport` DB cluster parameter] (aurora-mysql-require-secure-transport-parameter).
plan.table: Which control answers which question (columns: Question | Control): Who can reach the database port | a VPC security group: at first, the [firewall prevents any database access] (aurora-security-group-default-deny); Who can create or delete clusters | IAM policies ([you use AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)] (aurora-sec-iam-controls-management-actions)); Sign in without a password | IAM database authentication: [use an authentication token] (aurora-iam-db-auth-token-instead-of-password) with a [lifetime of 15 minutes] (aurora-iam-db-auth-token-sigv4-15-minutes); Data on disk | a KMS key chosen when you create the cluster. Then the Try it callout.
plan.why: Why is it cheap to turn on? Encryption is transparent: you [don't need to modify your database client applications] (aurora-encryption-transparent-no-client-changes).
plan.exam_signal: "encrypt an existing unencrypted Aurora cluster" points to a snapshot restored with a KMS key ([specify a KMS key when you restore] (aurora-restore-unencrypted-snapshot-specify-kms-key)); "all connections must use TLS" points to the engine's cluster parameter. Write the second clause without a second link if the trace already linked both parameter facts.

plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence: new clusters are now [encrypted by default with an AWS owned key] (aurora-change-default-encryption-new-clusters; volatile; it becomes a Changed recently entry only when the fact request is filled). Reference only: you [can't turn off encryption] (aurora-encryption-cannot-turn-off) and [can't change the KMS key] (aurora-encryption-kms-key-cannot-change); a blue/green deployment can also encrypt a cluster (aurora-sec-blue-green-encrypt-existing-cluster); a disabled key makes the cluster inaccessible (aurora-disabled-kms-key-cluster-inaccessible-recoverable); clusters must be in a VPC (aurora-security-vpc-required-security-group); public access needs every subnet of the group to be public (aurora-public-access-needs-all-public-subnets); Database Activity Streams send activity to Kinesis (aurora-das-pushes-to-kinesis; chapter 37); Kerberos with Directory Service (aurora-security-kerberos-with-directory-service).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: turn on encryption when you create the cluster, and require TLS in its parameter group. The thing to watch is old clusters: restore to encrypt.
plan.stop_and_answer: An unencrypted Aurora MySQL cluster must become encrypted. The team plans to add an encrypted Aurora Replica and then fail over to it. Will that work? sections.heading: FAQ quick-fire
sections.plan: Ten FAQ items in the form of CONVENTIONS D12 (see faq): a can-or-cannot question, the short answer with a fact link, then the verbatim AWS quote block from the item's FAQ page (the evidence page of its fact), holding the one whole sentence of the evidence quote that carries the answer. At most 430 words.

traps.belief: Each Aurora Replica keeps its own copy of the data, as an RDS read replica does, so every extra replica adds replication lag and storage cost.
traps.truth: Aurora Replicas connect to the same cluster volume as the writer; replica lag is usually much less than 100 milliseconds, and you pay for one copy of the storage.

traps.belief: An application can send its writes to the reader endpoint, so that the Aurora Replicas share the write load too.
traps.truth: The cluster endpoint is the only endpoint that performs write operations; a session on the reader endpoint runs read-only statements on an Aurora Replica.

traps.belief: Every Region of an Aurora global database accepts writes, as every replica of a DynamoDB global table does.
traps.truth: Only the primary cluster performs write operations; a secondary Region runs Aurora Replicas only, and write forwarding sends its writes to the primary.

traps.belief: When the primary Region of an Aurora global database has an outage, you run a switchover to move the primary role.
traps.truth: Switchovers are for global databases whose clusters are all healthy; to recover from an unplanned outage, you use the failover mechanism.

traps.belief: You can turn on encryption for an existing unencrypted Aurora cluster by modifying it.
traps.truth: You cannot convert an unencrypted DB cluster to an encrypted one; restore an unencrypted snapshot to a new cluster and specify a KMS key.

traps.belief: Because the cluster volume keeps six copies in three Availability Zones, a cluster with one DB instance is highly available and fails over in seconds.
traps.truth: The copies protect the data, not the compute: without an Aurora Replica, Aurora recreates the primary instance, which typically takes less than 10 minutes, and after an AZ outage you create new instances yourself.

traps.belief: The reader endpoint spreads every query evenly across the Aurora Replicas, also when the application keeps one long-lived connection pool.
traps.truth: The reader endpoint balances connections, not individual queries; to balance each query, the application opens a new connection for each query.

traps.belief: Aurora Auto Scaling adds capacity for writes when the writer is busy.
traps.truth: Aurora Auto Scaling adds and removes Aurora Replicas and helps only the reader instances; the writer keeps its instance class.

traps.belief: An idle Aurora Serverless v2 database costs nothing, whatever its settings.
traps.truth: Instances pause only when the minimum capacity is zero ACUs and no connection is open (RDS Proxy keeps one open); a minimum above zero never pauses, and storage is charged even while paused.

traps.belief: An Aurora PostgreSQL cluster can get a cross-Region read replica cluster, as Aurora MySQL can with binlog replication.
traps.truth: Aurora PostgreSQL does not support cross-Region Aurora Replicas; Aurora Global Database takes its reads and its recovery to other Regions.

traps.belief: A failover of an Aurora global database after a Region outage loses no data, because replication takes about a second.
traps.truth: Replication to the secondaries is asynchronous, so a failover can lose writes that were not replicated (RPO typically seconds); only a switchover of healthy clusters has an RPO of 0.

traps.belief: A point-in-time restore rolls the running Aurora cluster back, so the application keeps its endpoint.
traps.truth: A point-in-time or snapshot restore creates a new DB cluster with new endpoints; only Backtrack rewinds a cluster in place, and only on Aurora MySQL clusters created with Backtrack enabled.

traps.belief: Aurora I/O-Optimized always costs less, because it has no I/O charges.
traps.truth: I/O-Optimized is the best choice when I/O is 25% or more of the Aurora spend; below that share, Aurora Standard costs less.

traps.belief: To spread reads over Aurora Replicas, the application keeps the instance endpoint of each replica and chooses one itself, as it does with RDS read replicas.
traps.truth: The reader endpoint balances connections among all the Aurora Replicas, so the application does not hardcode hostnames or write its own balancing logic.

traps.belief: Amazon DynamoDB fits relational data that reports join across many tables, if each entity gets its own table.
traps.truth: Relational databases support complex queries through joins; removing joins is at the heart of NoSQL data modeling.

traps.belief: Amazon ElastiCache can be the only store of a system's records, because it is the fastest database.
traps.truth: The AWS decision guide describes ElastiCache as an ephemeral cache for frequently accessed data, a caching layer in front of a database.

traps.belief: Babelfish for Aurora PostgreSQL runs code written for any commercial engine, Oracle PL/SQL included, without changes.
traps.truth: Babelfish lets applications written for SQL Server work without code changes; for other engines AWS suggests AWS SCT to convert the schema and code.

traps.belief: Aurora can create a read replica of any source database, such as Oracle, and promote it to finish a migration.
traps.truth: Aurora brings in data from RDS for MySQL and RDS for PostgreSQL by snapshots or one-way replication; a source that is not PostgreSQL-compatible moves to Aurora PostgreSQL with AWS DMS.

traps.belief: You can encrypt an unencrypted Aurora cluster by adding an encrypted Aurora Replica and failing over to it.
traps.truth: You cannot create an encrypted Aurora Replica for an unencrypted DB cluster; restore a snapshot to a new cluster and specify a KMS key.

traps.belief: Moving reads from the writer to Aurora Replicas lowers the I/O charges of an Aurora Standard cluster.
traps.truth: I/O operations are counted the same way whether they run on a writer or a reader DB instance.

traps.belief: Aurora Serverless v2 instances have no I/O charges, so moving to them removes the I/O part of the bill.
traps.truth: Serverless instances use the storage configuration of their cluster, Aurora Standard or Aurora I/O-Optimized, like provisioned instances.

traps.belief: The lowest promotion tier keeps an Aurora Replica from ever becoming the writer.
traps.truth: Tiers set the order only: if the higher priority replicas are unhealthy or unavailable, Amazon RDS promotes the lower priority replica.

traps.belief: Aurora Serverless v2 is the most cost-effective capacity choice for every Aurora workload, a steady one included, because it scales with the load.
traps.truth: AWS describes Aurora Serverless v2 for variable or spiky workloads; provisioned clusters suit steady workloads, and Reserved Instances are appropriate for steady-state database workloads.

traps.belief: To move the primary role of an Aurora global database to another Region, you remove the secondary cluster from the global database and point the applications at it.
traps.truth: Removing a secondary cluster immediately stops replication and makes it a standalone cluster; a managed failover (after an outage) or a switchover (healthy clusters) moves the primary role, and Aurora switches the global writer endpoint.

traps.belief: Every migration into Aurora needs the AWS Schema Conversion Tool and AWS DMS, a migration from an RDS database of the same engine included.
traps.truth: AWS suggests AWS SCT when the source has a different engine; an RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance moves to Aurora PostgreSQL from a DB snapshot or through an Aurora read replica.

reasons_with_facts: Option 1 keeps the lag: RDS [copies them asynchronously to the read replica] (rds-read-replica-async-read-only) for each replica, each on its own storage ([Amazon RDS uses EBS volumes] (rds-storage-ebs-striping)), and with several replicas [it is up to your application] (rds-faq-read-replica-own-endpoint) to spread the reads.

Option 2: Aurora Replicas [connect to the same storage volume] (aurora-adding-replicas-read-same-volume-offload) with lag usually [much less than 100 milliseconds] (aurora-replica-lag-under-100-ms); one reader endpoint spreads read connections; Aurora fails over to a replica in [less than 60 seconds] (aurora-failover-time-with-replica-guide); the same [code, tools, and applications] (aurora-existing-mysql-postgres-code-works) keep working; and Aurora Global Database can [span multiple AWS Regions] (aurora-faq-global-db-definition) later, the path for PostgreSQL, which [doesn't support cross-Region Aurora Replicas] (aurora-postgres-no-cross-region-aurora-replicas).

question_slots.note: Shared stem: a company runs an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster with one writer and four Aurora Replicas: two large and two small. The team adds and removes replicas often. Each web request opens a new database connection. Changed phrase: 'Read-only queries from the web application must be spread across all the replicas, including replicas that are added later.' Ask: 'Which solution meets this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?' Key: (A) Connect the read-only queries to the reader endpoint of the cluster ([connection-balancing support for read-only connections] (aurora-reader-endpoint-connection-balancing-read-only); [reader endpoint for read-only connections] (aurora-ha-use-cluster-and-reader-endpoints)). Options identical in q07: (A) as above; (B) Create a custom endpoint that contains the two large replicas, and connect the read-only queries to it; (C) Point all connections of the application, writes included, at the reader endpoint, so that every replica shares the work (trap aurora-trap-writes-through-reader-endpoint in both stems; why links [the only one that can perform write operations] (aurora-cluster-endpoint-only-one-for-writes)); (D) Store the instance endpoint of each replica in the application settings, and choose one for each query (violates-qualifier in both stems: you then [hardcode all the hostnames] (aurora-endpoint-abstracts-connections-no-hardcode)). In q01, (B) is violates-requirement: the small replicas get no queries. 'Each web request opens a new connection' is in the shared stem so that connection balancing spreads the queries (no ambiguity with aurora-trap-reader-endpoint-balances-queries). Write option texts in neutral words that fit both stems.

Bullets also 2.1.K15, 3.3.S4. A company runs Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with three read replicas. At write peaks the replicas fall up to 40 seconds behind, and dashboards show stale data. The company needs a scalable read tier with replica lag in milliseconds, behind one read endpoint, without rewriting its SQL. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? Key: migrate to an Aurora PostgreSQL cluster and send dashboard queries to Aurora Replicas through the reader endpoint ([connect to the same storage volume] (aurora-adding-replicas-read-same-volume-offload); [much less than 100 milliseconds] (aurora-replica-lag-under-100-ms); [code, tools, and applications] (aurora-existing-mysql-postgres-code-works)). Distractors: stay on RDS, because Aurora Replicas also copy every change to their own storage, and add two larger read replicas (trap aurora-trap-replicas-copy-data; why links rds-read-replica-async-read-only and aurora-adding-replicas-read-same-volume-offload); convert the RDS DB instance to Multi-AZ and send the dashboard queries to the standby (trap rds-trap-standby-serves-reads; why links [doesn't serve read traffic] (rds-multi-az-instance-standby-no-reads)); put Amazon ElastiCache in front of all dashboard reads and keep the replicas (violates-qualifier: a second store to run and keep in step; why links dynamodb-decision-guide-elasticache-caching-layer). Do not offer a Multi-AZ DB cluster: its readable standbys could be argued.

Difficulty 1, qualifier none (no violates-qualifier option). Use Aurora PostgreSQL, so that Backtrack is not an answer. A faulty release deleted rows in an Aurora PostgreSQL cluster at 14:05; the backup retention period is 7 days. The company must get the data back as it was at 14:04 (a point in time). What should a solutions architect do? Key: restore the cluster to 14:04 as a new DB cluster, then copy the rows back ([any second during your retention period] (aurora-pitr-any-second-within-retention-period); [creating a new DB cluster] (aurora-pitr-creates-new-cluster)). Select TWO, five options. A company's application runs on AWS Lambda functions that use an Aurora PostgreSQL cluster with one writer and three Aurora Replicas. Keys: (1) put Amazon RDS Proxy between the functions and the cluster ([frequently open and close connections] (aurora-frequent-connections-use-rds-proxy); [exhaust database connection limits] (lambda-vpc-db-connections-rds-proxy)); (2) send the read-only queries to the reader endpoint ([reduces the overhead on the primary instance] (aurora-reader-endpoint-reduces-primary-overhead-scales-selects)). Alternative third distractor: raise max_connections far above what the application needs (misconception: [unused connections can cause performance to degrade] (aurora-postgres-unused-connections-degrade-performance)). Do not link the display that says 'we recommend'.

Distractors: a point-in-time restore of the existing cluster in place (trap aurora-trap-restore-in-place; why links aurora-pitr-creates-new-cluster); a point-in-time restore to a new cluster and a switch of the application (violates-qualifier and violates-requirement: new endpoint; restores [can take hours]: no such display; write 'is slower' and link [creating a new DB cluster] (aurora-pitr-creates-new-cluster)); create a clone of the cluster (misconception: a clone copies the current data, [shares the same data pages as the original] (aurora-clone-shares-data-pages-separate-volume)).
