speak.prompt: It is still PostgreSQL. What do I get from Aurora that RDS did not give me?
speak.note: Ben talks in short technical sentences and distrusts what he must run at night. Short answer: the same PostgreSQL, but on a storage layer that all instances share, so replicas stay milliseconds behind instead of forty seconds. How it works: the writer stores each change once, in six copies across three zones; Aurora Replicas read that same storage; one reader endpoint spreads the dashboard connections; if the writer fails, a replica takes over in under a minute behind the same endpoint. Watch: the bill changes shape: storage you use, and I/O per request on Aurora Standard; the move needs a short cutover. In your case: 'Which dashboards break first when the replica is behind?' Must not say: 'Aurora Replicas copy the data like RDS replicas'; 'replica lag is zero'; 'Aurora is a different engine, so you rewrite the SQL'. Numbers as words from the say forms: well under a hundred milliseconds; fifteen Aurora Replicas besides the primary; under a minute; six copies, three Availability Zones.

speak.persona: a startup founder in office hours
speak.prompt: Aurora Serverless v2 or a provisioned instance: which one should our new SaaS database use?
speak.note: First sentence starts 'Both': both run the same Aurora engine on the same storage; the difference is how capacity is sized. Short answer: Serverless v2 while the load is new and uneven; provisioned, with Reserved Instances, once it is steady. How it works: Serverless v2 grows and shrinks the instance in small steps inside a range you set, even with connections open; a provisioned instance has a fixed size that you choose. Watch: the minimum you set decides the idle cost; one cluster can mix both, so you can switch later. In your case: 'Do you know your peak yet, and how often does it come?' Must not say: 'serverless is always cheaper'; 'serverless means no instance'; 'you must rebuild the cluster to change'. Numbers as words: about two gibibytes of memory per ACU.

speak.prompt: Aurora Global Database or DynamoDB global tables: which one gives us a second Region?
speak.note: First sentence starts 'Both': both keep a copy of your data in another Region; the difference is who can write. Short answer: Aurora Global Database if the data is relational; DynamoDB global tables if every Region must write. How it works: Aurora has one writer Region and read-only secondaries, replicated in about a second, and you fail over after an outage; in a global table every Region reads and writes, and no database failover is needed. Watch: an Aurora failover can lose a few seconds of writes; DynamoDB needs a key-value design without joins. In your case: 'Do your users in the second Region need to write, or mostly read?' Must not say: 'every Aurora Region accepts writes'; 'Aurora failover loses nothing'; 'DynamoDB supports joins'. Numbers as words: typically under one second; a few seconds of possible data loss.

speak.prompt: Ben wants to pay for I/O-Optimized on our main database. Is it worth it?
speak.note: Ana uses no AWS terms: explain I/O the first time as 'each time the database reads or writes a piece of data on disk'. Short answer: it depends on one number on the bill: the share of I/O charges. How it works: on the standard plan we pay for each I/O request; on I/O-Optimized I/O has no charge; AWS calls it the best choice at a quarter or more of the database spend. Watch: we can go back to the standard plan at any time, but move to I/O-Optimized only once every thirty days, so decide from a full month of bills. In your case: 'Can finance pull last month's database bill split by item?' Must not say: 'I/O-Optimized is always cheaper'; 'I/O-Optimized makes the database faster'; 'we can switch back and forth every week'. Numbers as words: a quarter or more; once every thirty days.

cards.front: In Aurora, how many Aurora Replicas can one DB cluster have?
cards.back: Up to 15 Aurora Replicas in addition to the primary DB instance.

cards.front: In Aurora, how many copies of the data does the cluster volume keep?
cards.back: Six copies, across three Availability Zones.

cards.front: In Aurora, how long does a failover to an Aurora Replica typically take?
cards.back: Less than 60 seconds, often less than 30 seconds.

cards.front: In Aurora, a cluster has no Aurora Replica. How long does recovery typically take?
cards.back: Less than 10 minutes: Aurora recreates the primary.

cards.front: In Aurora, how far behind the writer is an Aurora Replica usually?
cards.back: Much less than 100 milliseconds.

cards.front: In Aurora Global Database, what is the typical replication latency to a secondary Region?
cards.back: Typically under a second.

cards.front: In Aurora Global Database, how fast does AWS say a secondary Region can be promoted?
cards.back: In less than 1 minute.

cards.front: In Aurora, what is the range of the backup retention period?
cards.back: 1–35 days.

cards.front: Aurora Replica or RDS read replica: which one reads the writer's own storage volume?
cards.back: The Aurora Replica.

cards.front: In Aurora, cluster endpoint or reader endpoint: which one accepts writes?
cards.back: The cluster endpoint.

cards.front: In Aurora, the load is spiky and hard to predict. Which capacity option fits?
cards.back: Aurora Serverless v2: capacity follows the load inside your range.

cards.front: A relational database must recover in another Region with an RPO of seconds. What do you use?
cards.back: Aurora Global Database.

cards.front: In an Aurora global database, can a secondary cluster accept writes on its own?
cards.back: No. Only the primary cluster writes; write forwarding sends writes there.

cards.front: In Aurora, can you turn on encryption for an existing unencrypted cluster?
cards.back: No. Restore a snapshot to a new cluster with a KMS key.

cards.front: In Aurora Global Database, failover or switchover: which one is for a Region outage?
cards.back: Failover. Switchover needs healthy clusters.

cards.front: In Aurora Global Database, is a failover after a Region outage free of data loss?
cards.back: No. Writes that were not yet replicated can be lost.

cards.front: In Aurora, can Aurora Auto Scaling add capacity for writes?
cards.back: No. It scales only the reader instances.

cards.front: In Aurora, does the reader endpoint balance each query?
cards.back: No. It balances connections, not individual queries.

cards.front: In Aurora Serverless v2, does an instance pause if the minimum capacity is above zero ACUs?
cards.back: No. It pauses only with a minimum of zero ACUs.

cards.front: Can an Aurora PostgreSQL cluster have a cross-Region Aurora Replica?
cards.back: No. Use Aurora Global Database.

cards.front: In Aurora, does a point-in-time restore roll back the running cluster?
cards.back: No. It creates a new DB cluster.

cards.front: In Aurora, I/O is a large share of the database bill. Which storage configuration fits?
cards.back: Aurora I/O-Optimized, from 25% or more of the spend.

cards.front: In Aurora, can you turn off automated backups?
cards.back: No. They are always on.

cards.front: In Aurora, reports must run only on two large replicas. What do the reports connect to?
cards.back: A custom endpoint with those two replicas.

cards.front: Can you backtrack an Aurora PostgreSQL cluster?
cards.back: No. Backtrack is an Aurora MySQL feature.

cards.front: In Aurora, you need a test copy of production data within minutes. What do you use?
cards.back: An Aurora clone: it stores only changed pages.

cards.front: Moving Oracle to Aurora PostgreSQL: which tool converts the schema?
cards.back: AWS Schema Conversion Tool (AWS SCT).

cards.front: RDS for PostgreSQL to Aurora, same account and Region, short cutover: which path?
cards.back: An Aurora read replica, promoted at zero lag.

cards.front: Aurora Global Database or DynamoDB global tables: which one accepts writes in every Region?
cards.back: DynamoDB global tables.

cards.front: In Aurora Serverless v2, a dev database is idle most of the week. How do you stop paying for its compute?
cards.back: Set the minimum capacity to zero ACUs, so it pauses.

cards.front: In Aurora, does a new DB instance get its own copy of the data?
cards.back: No. It connects to the shared cluster volume.

cards.front: In Aurora, a restorable copy must be kept for many years. What do you use?
cards.back: Manual DB cluster snapshots: they do not expire.

diagrams.title: A write, the shared volume, the replicas and a failover
diagrams.claim: Writes go through the writer into one volume with six copies, and the Aurora Replicas read that same volume.
diagrams.alt: A sequence with four participants: an application, the writer DB instance, the cluster volume in three Availability Zones, and an Aurora Replica. The application writes through the cluster endpoint, the writer stores the change in the volume, the replica reads the same volume for queries that come through the reader endpoint, and after a failure the replica becomes the writer.
say: The application sends writes to the cluster endpoint, which connects to the current primary DB instance.
Aurora synchronously replicates the data across Availability Zones to six storage nodes.
Read-only connections use the reader endpoint, which spreads them among the Aurora Replicas.
Aurora Replicas connect to the same storage volume as the writer, so no data is copied to them.
If the writer fails, Aurora automatically fails over to an Aurora Replica, and the cluster endpoint follows it.
